title: Slow blink

brief.story: The bench's standby line should rise slowly when you press the button, taking about a second, so whatever it drives fades in instead of snapping on. The capacitor is fitted, with a 100 kΩ bleed resistor that empties it when you let go. The resistor that sets the timing isn't.
brief.goal: Make C1 charge to 63 % of its final voltage in 0.8–1.2 s after you press SW1. Hold the button and watch it on the scope.

hints: The timing resistor goes from the button's output (column 6) to C1's + leg (column 14). The current through it is what charges the capacitor.
The time constant τ = R × C is how long a capacitor takes to charge to 63 % of its final voltage.
For τ = 1 s with C = 100 µF: R = 1 s / 0.0001 F = 10 kΩ.
debrief: A capacitor can't change its voltage instantly: it fills through the resistor, fast at first and slower as it fills up. After one time constant, τ = R × C, it's at 63 %; after five it's practically full. The 100 kΩ bleed resistor steals a little of the charging current, which is why the scope shows about 0.9 s instead of exactly 1. RC timing is how circuits make delays, debounce buttons and blink LEDs without a microcontroller.
